title: What Happens on Education After the Midterms?
author: Charlie Barone
summary: With the midterms six weeks away, Charlie Barone reviews four recent K-12 agendas from the left and center-left: the Progressive Policy Institute's compact by Rachel Canter, Third Way's report by Ellie Cash, Josh Cowen's two pieces on national and gubernatorial plans, and Jennifer Berkshire's mom-populist argument in The New Republic. He finds total consensus only in opposing private school vouchers and ESAs, with sharp divergence on public school choice, the federal scholarship tax credit, and above all assessment and accountability. PPI and Third Way embrace traditional centrist reforms and the science of reading, while Cowen is pragmatic and union-friendly and Berkshire defends the status quo. Barone praises Cowen's advice that governors pick five things and win, and criticizes Berkshire for treating accountability as the enemy. He concludes that Democrats need a coherent, evidence-driven governing plan that goes beyond more funding.
points: All four proposals oppose private school vouchers and ESAs, the only point of complete consensus.
Assessment and accountability mark the sharpest divide, with PPI closest to the No Child Left Behind model.
Canter goes furthest on the science of reading, drawing on Mississippi's literacy success.
Third Way alone gives sustained attention to artificial intelligence and builds its case on polling.
Barone argues parents want the system fixed, which requires measurement, transparency, and sometimes consequences for adults.
quotes: The midterm elections are exactly six weeks away, with implications not only for control of the U.S. House and Senate but also for 39 governorships and more than a dozen state legislatures.
In a rare point of total consensus, all four oppose private-school vouchers and ESAs.
Assessments and Accountability. This is the sharpest reform-vs-establishment divide.
Cowen asserts that a blue state governor staring down a red legislature doesn’t need a manifesto, they just need to “pick five things and win.
But you can’t build a “mom populist” message on defending the status quo when the status quo includes chronic absenteeism, high rates of college remediation, and NAEP scores nobody’s proud of.
Parents aren’t nostalgic for a system that didn’t work in the first place. They want the system fixed, and “fixed” requires measurement, transparency, and yes, sometimes consequences for adults.

The party that treats this as a message contest may win a news cycle. The party that treats it as a governing problem will win the next decade of NAEP releases, postsecondary success, and economic mobility
